Foundations: Clear Writing, the Right Tone and the Phone

Every business message, from a WhatsApp reply to a formal letter, rests on the same three habits: say what you want early, use plain words, and match your tone to the reader. This module builds those habits and applies them to the most common business channel of all, the phone call.

Business readers are busy. A supplier, a customer or a programme officer often reads your message on a small phone screen, between other tasks. If they cannot see within a few seconds **what you want and by when**, your message waits, or it is misunderstood. Clear writing is not about big English. It is about making the reader's job easy.
A woman composing a message on a screen
Before you type, decide the one thing you want the reader to know or do.
Rule 1: Main point first

Many of us were taught to build up slowly: greetings, background, history, and only at the end the request. In business, turn this around. Put the **purpose and the request in the first one or two sentences**, then give only the background the reader needs. Some writers call this BLUF, short for "bottom line up front". The polite greeting still comes first, but it stays short.
Rule 2: Plain words and short sentences

Plain language means words your reader understands the first time. Government plain-language guides, such as the United States plainlanguage.gov guidelines, recommend short sentences, everyday words, and speaking directly to the reader as "you". This matters even more when your reader speaks English as a second or third language, which is common across Nigeria and Africa. Aim for sentences of about 15 to 20 words, and one idea per sentence.

Notice the last two rows. "Do the needful" and "revert" are common in Nigerian offices, but they hide the actual action. A reader from another country may not understand "revert" as "reply" at all. Always name the exact action and, where possible, a date.
Rule 3: Active voice

In the **active voice**, the person doing the action comes first: "Chika will deliver the chairs on Monday." In the **passive voice**, the doer is hidden or comes last: "The chairs will be delivered." By whom? Passive sentences are not always wrong, but in business they often hide responsibility. Use the active voice when you want someone to act.

Worked example: a message to a hall manager, before and after
For example, Funke runs a small events business in Ibadan. She needs to confirm a hall booking for a client's birthday party and wants the hall manager to send the invoice.

Before (68 words): "Good afternoon sir, I hope this message finds you well. I am writing in respect of the discussion we had last week concerning the possibility of using your hall for an event which a client of mine is planning towards the end of the month, and I wanted to find out whether it would be possible for you to kindly do the needful regarding the invoice at your earliest convenience."
Problem 1: the request (send the invoice) is hidden at the very end.
Problem 2: no date, no hall name, no number of guests, so the manager must call back to ask.
Problem 3: "do the needful" and "at your earliest convenience" give no clear action or deadline.

After (45 words): "Good afternoon Mr Bello. Please send me the invoice for the Main Hall for Saturday 29 March, 2pm to 8pm, for about 120 guests. My client will pay the deposit once I receive it. Could you send it by Wednesday? Thank you, Funke Adeyemi, 0803 000 0000."
The second version is shorter, puts the request first, and gives every detail the manager needs to act without calling back.

Short paragraphs and lists

On a phone screen, a paragraph of ten lines looks like a wall of text, and readers skip it. Keep paragraphs to about three or four lines. When you give several items, such as sizes, dates or documents, put them in a short list. A list lets the reader tick off each point, and it makes it obvious if something is missing. For example, "Please bring: 1. CAC certificate, 2. a valid ID, 3. two passport photos" is easier to act on than the same items buried in a long sentence.

Tone is how your message sounds in the reader's head. The same request can sound respectful, cold, pushy or desperate depending on the words around it. In person, your smile and voice soften your words. In writing, the reader only has the words, so tone must be built in on purpose.

The formality ladder

Think of formality as a ladder. At the bottom are people you know well and deal with often. At the top are people and organisations you are meeting for the first time, or who have authority over a decision you need. **The higher the step, the more formal you write.** When you are not sure, start one step higher, then follow the other person's lead once they reply.

Titles and respect in the Nigerian setting

Titles carry real weight in many Nigerian and African business settings. If someone signs as Dr, Chief, Alhaji, Engr. or Barrister, use that title until they invite you to drop it. With an older person or a senior official, "Sir" or "Ma" in a spoken conversation is normal and polite. In a written email, "Dear Dr Okeke" carries the same respect without repeating "sir" in every line. When writing to someone abroad, use Mr or Ms with their surname unless they sign with a first name only.
Firm is not the same as rude

Sometimes you must ask for something difficult: late payment, a missed delivery, a wrong order. You can be firm without being rude. A firm message states the facts, the effect, and the exact next step. A rude message attacks the person, uses capital letters to shout, or makes threats you will not carry out.
Worked example: chasing a late delivery, three tones
For example, Amina ordered 50 branded tote bags from a printer in Kano for a conference. The printer promised delivery on Monday. It is now Wednesday and nothing has arrived.
Too soft: "Good day sir, sorry to disturb you, please whenever you have time, maybe you can check on the bags? No problem if not." The printer reads this as "not urgent".
Too harsh: "WHERE ARE MY BAGS?? You people are never serious. If they don't come today I will report you everywhere." The printer becomes defensive, and the relationship is damaged.

Firm and polite: "Good morning Mr Sani. The 50 tote bags (order 112) were due on Monday and have not arrived. The conference starts on Saturday, so I need them by Thursday 5pm. Can you confirm today whether that is possible? Thank you."
The firm version gives the order number, the original date, the reason for urgency, a clear deadline and a direct question that needs an answer today.
The printer replies with a real delivery time instead of an excuse, and Amina keeps a supplier she may need again.
Text loses your smile

Short replies such as "Ok." or "Noted." can read as cold or annoyed, even when you are just busy. Add a few words: "Noted, thank you. I will send it by 4pm." Avoid all capital letters, many exclamation marks, and emojis in first contact or formal messages.
Match, then lead

A useful habit is to **match the other person's level**, then lead slightly towards clarity. If a new partner writes "Dear Mrs Eze", reply with "Dear Mr Daniel", not "Hi!". If a long-time customer sends a voice note in Pidgin, a friendly reply in simple English or Pidgin is fine, but put the price, quantity and delivery day in clear written text so there is a record. Being friendly and being exact are not opposites.
Saying no and apologising politely

Two of the hardest tone moments are refusing a request and admitting a mistake. In both cases, be brief, warm and specific. Thank the person, give the answer clearly, give a short reason if it helps, and offer an alternative where you can. Avoid long, nervous explanations; they make a simple no sound uncertain.
Refusing a discount: "Thank you for asking. Our price for this order is fixed at ₦45,000, but delivery within Ikeja is free."
Declining a job: "Thank you for thinking of us. We are fully booked that weekend, but I can recommend a colleague."
Apologising: "I am sorry, I sent the wrong invoice. The correct one is attached and the total is ₦32,000."
The newer or more senior the reader, the more formal you write.
When unsure, start one step more formal and follow their lead.
Use the titles people use for themselves.
Firm messages state facts, effect and next step, without insults or threats.
Very short replies can sound cold; add a few warm, clear words.

For many small businesses in Nigeria, the phone is still the main business tool. Customers call to ask prices, suppliers call about deliveries, and partners prefer a quick call to a long email. A well-handled call builds trust fast. A rushed or confusing call can lose a sale in under a minute.
A woman talking on a mobile phone

Answering a business call

When a call comes to your business line, answer within a few rings with three things: a greeting, your business name and your own name. For example: "Good morning, Bisi's Bakes, this is Bisi speaking. How can I help you?" This tells the caller they reached the right place and who they are speaking to. If you are in a noisy market or driving, it is more professional to let the call go and call back within the hour than to shout "I can't hear you!".
Greet, give the business name and your name.
Listen to the full request without interrupting.
Repeat the key details back: "So that is two dozen cupcakes for Friday at 10am?"
Agree the next step: price, payment method, delivery time.
Close politely and say what happens next: "I will send the invoice on WhatsApp in ten minutes."
Making a call: the three-part script

Before you call a supplier, client or official, write three short lines: **who you are, why you are calling, and what you need from them**. Keep your notebook and any order numbers in front of you. This avoids the common problem of talking for five minutes and ending the call without the answer you needed.

The call is not finished until the agreement is in writing.
Worked example: calling a fabric supplier
For example, Esther makes school uniforms in Aba and needs to confirm a price before she quotes a school.
Her three lines: "Esther, Uniform Works, ordered from you in January. Calling to confirm the price of navy gabardine for 300 yards. I need the price and delivery date today so I can quote a school."
On the call: "Good afternoon, this is Esther from Uniform Works. I bought navy gabardine from you in January. I am calling to confirm your current price for 300 yards and how soon you can deliver."
The supplier says about ₦2,500 per yard (an illustrative price), delivery in five days.
Esther repeats it back: "So 300 yards at ₦2,500, that is ₦750,000 in total, delivered by next Tuesday?"
Within ten minutes she sends a WhatsApp message: "Thank you for the call. Confirming: 300 yards navy gabardine at ₦2,500 per yard, total ₦750,000, delivery by Tuesday 18 March. Please confirm."
Esther now has a written record she can rely on when she quotes the school, and any misunderstanding about price is caught before money moves.
Voicemails and voice notes

Voice notes on WhatsApp are fast and personal, and many customers prefer them. But a three-minute voice note is hard to search, hard to listen to in a meeting, and impossible to skim. Keep business voice notes **under about one minute**, say the main point first, and follow up any numbers, addresses or account details in text. For a voicemail, say your name, business, reason for calling and phone number slowly, and repeat the number at the end.

Phone scams

Never share your BVN, card PIN, OTP codes or online banking password on a call, even if the caller says they are from your bank. Banks do not ask for these. End the call and phone your bank on the number printed on your card or their official website.
Taking a message for someone else
If a call is for a colleague or partner who is not available, never just say "She is not around" and end the call. Take a proper message so that nothing is lost.
Say politely that the person is not available and offer to take a message.

Write the phone number and read it back digit by digit.
Note the reason for the call and how urgent it is.
Tell the caller when they can expect a call back, and pass the message on in writing straight away.

Finally, if you miss a business call, return it the same day where possible. A quick message such as "Sorry I missed your call, I am in a meeting until 3pm. Can I call you then?" keeps the customer warm.

The subject line

The subject line decides whether and when your email is opened. Make it **specific**: what it is about and, if needed, what you want. "Hello" or "Enquiry" tells the reader nothing. "Quotation request: 200 branded mugs, needed by 30 April" tells them everything before they open it.

The five parts of a business email
Purpose sentence
Key details

Every business email can follow this order, from a two-line note to a full proposal cover email.
Greeting: "Dear Mrs Okoro," for formal, "Good morning Tunde," for a known contact.
Purpose sentence: one sentence saying why you are writing.
Key details: only what the reader needs, using short paragraphs or a short list.
Clear request: what you want them to do and by when, ideally as a question.
Closing and signature: "Kind regards," then your full name, role, business name, phone number.
To, CC and BCC

Put the person who must **act** in the To line. Put people who only need to **know** in CC (carbon copy). Use BCC (blind carbon copy) when you email many people who do not know each other, such as customers, so that their addresses stay private. Sending a group email to 50 customers with every address visible in the To line exposes their contact details to everyone on the list. Before you click Reply All, ask whether everyone really needs your reply.
Worked example: a first email to a potential corporate client
For example, Ngozi runs a small catering business in Lagos and has been told that a logistics company buys lunch packs for staff training days.
Subject: "Lunch packs for staff training days: menu and price list attached"
Greeting: "Dear Mrs Adebayo,"
Purpose: "Mr Kola Ojo of your HR team suggested I contact you about lunch packs for your monthly staff training days."

Details: "We supply packed lunches for groups of 20 to 150 in Lagos Mainland. Our standard pack is jollof rice, chicken and a drink, about ₦3,500 per pack at current prices. We have served three corporate clients this year. Our menu and price list are attached as one PDF."
Request: "Could we arrange a free tasting for two members of your team next week? I am available Tuesday or Thursday afternoon."
Signature: "Kind regards, Ngozi Eze, Founder, Ngozi's Kitchen, 0805 000 0000, CAC-registered business."
In about 110 words, Mrs Adebayo knows who referred Ngozi, what she offers, the price range and exactly what Ngozi is asking for.

When you send an important email and hear nothing, do not assume the answer is no. People are busy and emails get buried.

The complete reply

Most customer enquiries ask the same few questions: Is it available? How much? How do I pay? When can I get it? A **complete reply** answers all four in one message, so the customer can decide without a long back and forth. Every extra message you make them send is a chance for them to buy elsewhere.
A complete customer reply
Greet by name
Confirm availability
Give price and options
Explain payment and delivery
Ask one clear question
One message that covers these five points usually turns an enquiry into an order.
Worked example: answering "How much?", before and after
For example, Halima sells hand-made bead necklaces from Abuja. A new customer sends: "Hello, how much is the blue necklace in your status?"
Before: "8k". The customer must now ask about delivery, payment and whether it is still available, and may simply leave.

After: "Good afternoon Joy, thank you for asking. Yes, the blue beaded necklace is available. It is ₦8,000. Matching earrings are ₦3,000 extra. Delivery within Abuja is about ₦2,000 and takes 1 to 2 days. You can pay by bank transfer and I will send the account details. Would you like the necklace alone or with the earrings?"
The customer replies: "With earrings please."
Halima confirms in writing: "Great. Order: blue necklace ₦8,000 + earrings ₦3,000 + delivery ₦2,000 = ₦13,000. Please send your delivery address and phone number."
One complete reply and one written confirmation turn a two-word enquiry into a confirmed ₦13,000 order with no confusion about the total.
Broadcasts, status and respect

A **broadcast list** sends one message to many customers, each receiving it as a private chat. Broadcast messages only reach people who have saved your number in their phone, which is WhatsApp's built-in way of keeping broadcasts to people who know you. Use broadcasts for genuine news: new stock, price changes, holiday hours. Sending several promotions a day, or adding people to groups without asking, quickly leads to people blocking or reporting your number.
Payment and privacy safety on WhatsApp

Never deliver goods on the strength of a screenshot of a transfer alone; check your own banking app or SMS alert from your bank. Never send customers' phone numbers or addresses to other people. Turn on two-step verification in WhatsApp settings so no one can take over your business account with a stolen code.

In British-style English, which Nigerian business writing generally follows, the rule is simple: if you began with the person's **name** ("Dear Mr Bello"), end with **"Yours sincerely"**. If you began with **"Dear Sir or Madam"**, end with **"Yours faithfully"**. American writers often use "Sincerely" for both. Whichever you use, be consistent.
Worked example: a complaint letter, before and after
For example, Grace owns a small printing shop in Enugu. A generator she bought from a dealer stopped working after two weeks, and her calls have not been answered.

Before: "I am very disappointed with your company. The generator you sold me is useless and I want my money back immediately or I will take action." No date of purchase, no receipt number, no model, no clear request.
After, opening paragraph: "I am writing about a 3.5 kVA generator, receipt number 0458, which I bought from your Ogui Road branch on 2 March 2025."

Details paragraph: "The generator stopped starting on 16 March. I called your branch on 17 and 18 March and was told a technician would visit, but no one has come. A copy of the receipt and the warranty card is enclosed."
Request paragraph: "Please arrange a repair or replacement under the warranty by Friday 28 March. You can reach me on 0807 000 0000."
Close: "Yours faithfully," signature, "Grace Nwosu, Owner, Grace Prints", because she opened with "Dear Sir or Madam".

Trust is built slowly and lost quickly. In business communication, three things damage trust more than anything else: promising what you cannot deliver, being careless with other people's information, and responding badly when something goes wrong. This lesson gives you practical habits for all three.

Promise only what you can deliver

It is tempting to say yes to a big order or a fast deadline to win the job. But a written promise, whether a price, a quantity or a delivery date, is something the customer will plan around and may hold you to. Before you commit in writing, check your stock, your suppliers, your time and your cash. If you are not sure, say what you **can** commit to and when you will confirm the rest.

Confidentiality and personal data

Customers trust you with their names, phone numbers, addresses and sometimes payment details. Nigeria's **Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023**, overseen by the Nigeria Data Protection Commission, sets rules for how organisations collect and use personal data. Even as a small business, the safe habits are simple: collect only what you need, use it only for the reason you collected it, keep it secure, and do not share it without permission.
Do not forward a customer's phone number or address to anyone who does not need it to deliver their order.
Do not post screenshots of customer chats or receipts showing names, numbers or account details.
Do not tell one client about another client's prices, orders or problems.
Lock your phone and laptop with a PIN or password, and turn on two-step verification for WhatsApp and email.
Handling a complaint: the LAST method

Complaints are a chance to keep a customer for life, or to lose them and everyone they talk to. A widely taught customer-service approach is often summarised as **LAST**: Listen, Apologise, Solve, Thank. Apologising for the customer's experience is not the same as admitting legal fault; it shows you take them seriously.
The LAST complaint method
Listen fully
Apologise sincerely
Solve with a clear offer
Thank and follow up
Work through each step in order, and the follow-up brings the customer back to trusting you.
Worked example: replying to an angry customer
For example, Blessing sells baked goods in Warri. A customer sends: "The cake you delivered for my daughter's birthday was squashed and the writing was spoilt. I am very disappointed."
Listen: Blessing reads the whole message, asks for a photo, and does not argue about the delivery rider.
Apologise: "I am truly sorry, Mrs Efe. Your daughter's birthday cake should have arrived perfect, and I understand how disappointing this was."
Solve: "I would like to make it right. I can refund 50% (₦12,500 of the ₦25,000) today, or bake a fresh cake of the same size free of charge for any date you choose. Which would you prefer?"
Thank: "Thank you for telling me directly. It helps me fix our packaging." She later changes to a sturdier box and checks every cake before it leaves.
Follow up: a week later she messages: "I hope the replacement cake was enjoyed. Thank you again for giving us another chance."
The customer chooses the replacement cake, stays loyal, and Blessing fixes the real cause of the problem.
Delivering bad news

If a delivery will be late or a price must rise, tell the customer **as early as possible**, with the reason in one sentence, the new plan and what you are doing to help. "Your order will arrive Thursday instead of Tuesday because our supplier's truck broke down. I have arranged express delivery at no extra cost." Silence, followed by excuses after the deadline, does far more damage.
Stay professional when others are not

If someone insults you in a message, do not reply in anger. Wait, then reply calmly with facts and a next step. Your written replies can be screenshotted and shared, so write every message as if others may one day read it.

Closing warmly: "Thank you for your patience. We value your business."

Every business negotiates all the time: with suppliers on price, with landlords on rent, with customers on discounts, with partners on who does what. Negotiation is not about shouting or tricks. Good negotiation is mostly **preparation, listening and clear communication**, so both sides leave with an agreement they will keep.

The principled negotiation method

One of the best-known approaches comes from Roger Fisher and William Ury of the Harvard Negotiation Project, in their book **Getting to Yes**. They describe four principles. First, **separate the people from the problem**: be respectful to the person while being firm on the issue. Second, **focus on interests, not positions**. Third, **invent options for mutual gain** before deciding. Fourth, **insist on objective criteria**, such as market prices or published rates, rather than pressure.
Positions and interests

A **position** is what someone says they want: "I want ₦50,000 off." An **interest** is why they want it: "My cash is tight this month" or "I need to stay within my client's budget." When you find the interest, you can often find a solution that the position hides, such as splitting payment, changing the quantity or adjusting delivery.

The term **BATNA** comes from Getting to Yes. The stronger your alternative, the more confidently you can negotiate, because you do not need this particular deal. Always find at least one real alternative before an important negotiation. (All prices here are illustrative only.)

Worked example: negotiating a bulk fabric price
For example, Zainab makes ready-to-wear dresses in Kaduna and buys Ankara fabric from one wholesaler. She wants a better price for a larger, regular order. All figures are illustrative.
Preparation: current price about ₦9,000 per 6-yard piece. Target ₦8,200. Walk-away ₦8,600. BATNA: another wholesaler in the same market quoted ₦8,500, but with slower delivery.
Opening: "I have bought from you for a year and I am planning to order 50 pieces every month instead of 20. Could you give me a price of ₦8,000 per piece for that volume?"
Listening: the wholesaler says ₦8,000 is too low because he must pay for transport from Lagos. Zainab asks: "What would help you most?" He says: payment on time and fewer small orders.
Options: Zainab offers to pay the full amount on collection and order once a month. He offers ₦8,300.
Agreement: they settle at ₦8,300 for orders of 50 pieces or more, paid on collection. Saving: (₦9,000 − ₦8,300) × 50 = ₦35,000 per month.
Written summary on WhatsApp: "Thank you. Confirming: 50 pieces or more per month at ₦8,300 per piece, full payment on collection, starting April."
By understanding the wholesaler's interest in reliable payment and fewer small orders, Zainab reached a price inside her target range and a written agreement both can rely on.

To understand interests: "What matters most to you in this order?"
To use objective criteria: "Other suppliers in the market are quoting around ₦8,500. How can we get closer?"
To trade, not give away: "If I pay in full on collection, can you do ₦8,300?"
To pause: "Let me think about this and reply by tomorrow at noon."
Silence and time are allowed

You do not have to answer an offer immediately. Saying "Let me check my numbers and get back to you by tomorrow" is professional and protects you from agreeing to something below your walk-away point.

Giving a discount without asking for anything in return, such as faster payment or a bigger order.
Making personal attacks or showing anger, which turns a problem into a quarrel.
Leaving the agreement only verbal, so each side remembers it differently a month later.

High-context and low-context communication

The anthropologist Edward T. Hall described cultures as tending towards **high-context** or **low-context** communication. In high-context settings, much of the meaning is in the relationship, the setting and what is not said directly. In low-context settings, people expect meaning to be stated plainly in the words themselves. Many West African business settings lean towards high context; many Northern European and American business settings lean towards low context. These are tendencies, not rules about every person.

Time zones and timing

Nigeria uses **West Africa Time (WAT)**, which is one hour ahead of Coordinated Universal Time (UTC+1), with no daylight saving changes. The United Kingdom is one hour behind Nigeria in winter and the same time as Nigeria in summer, because the UK changes its clocks. The east coast of the United States is five or six hours behind Nigeria, depending on the season. When you propose a call abroad, **state both times**.
Worked example: scheduling a call with a buyer abroad
For example, Chiamaka exports shea butter from Abuja and needs a video call with a buyer in New York in winter, when New York is six hours behind Nigeria.
Her working hours: 9am to 6pm WAT. Converted to New York in winter: 3am to 12 noon.
A good overlap: 3pm WAT is 9am in New York, early in the buyer's day.
Her message: "Dear Ms Carter, could we have a 30-minute video call on Tuesday 14 January at 9am New York time (3pm in Nigeria, WAT)? I will send a Google Meet link."
She checks the time in a world clock app before sending, and adds the call to her calendar with both times.
Deadline wording: "Please send the signed order by Friday 17 January, 5pm New York time."
Because both times are stated, neither side misses the call or a deadline because of a time difference.

When unsure, be polite, clear and patient, ask questions rather than assume, and follow the other person's lead on formality, greetings and directness. Most people welcome a sincere effort to understand their style.

Learn how people want to be addressed and how to pronounce their names; asking politely is a sign of respect, not ignorance. With international contacts, a short, friendly greeting is usually enough before moving to the agenda.

Speak a little more slowly than usual and pause for questions.
Send a short written summary after the call, because spoken accents can make details easy to mishear.

Why this matters
Three habits behind every good message
Say what you want early

Your reader often sees your message on a small phone screen, between other tasks. If they cannot see quickly what you want and by when, your message waits.
So the first habit is to say what you want early.
The second is plain words. Clear writing is not about big English.
The third is to match your tone to the reader.
And we finish with the phone, still the main business tool for many of us.
Step by step
Name the exact action and a date. Not "do the needful".
Before you type, ask: who is reading this?
Then ask: what exactly must they do?
Now put the purpose and the request in the first one or two sentences. Keep the greeting, but keep it short.
Finally, check and cut. Aim for sentences of about 15 to 20 words, with one idea in each.
Watch out for phrases like do the needful, or kindly revert. They hide the real action. Say please send the signed form, or please reply by Friday.
Worked example
Funke's message to the hall manager
Before: 68 words
Request hidden at the very end
No date, hall or number of guests
"Do the needful", no deadline
After: 45 words
Asks for the invoice first
Main Hall, Saturday, about 120 guests
Asks for it by Wednesday
Name and phone number at the end
For example, Funke runs an events business in Ibadan and needs the hall manager to send an invoice.
Her first message was 68 words, with the request hidden at the end and no date, hall name or number of guests.
Her new message is 45 words. Please send me the invoice for the Main Hall for Saturday, for about 120 guests, by Wednesday.
The manager can act without calling back.
The higher the step, the more formal
Think of formality as a ladder. At the top are banks, government and anyone you contact for the first time. Write in full sentences, with no emojis.
Next come new clients and partners. Be polite and complete, with a little warmth.
Regular suppliers and customers can be friendly and short, but still clear on details.
Team members get brief messages, but still with the task and deadline.
When unsure, start one step higher, then follow their lead.

Capital letters, insults and threats. The printer becomes defensive and the relationship is damaged.
Order number, the date it was due, why it is urgent, a clear deadline and a direct question.
Firm is not the same as rude. For example, Amina's 50 tote bags from a printer in Kano were due on Monday. It is now Wednesday.

Three written channels you use most

Email is still the main formal channel for banks, grant programmes, larger companies and government. Your email is often the first thing they see of your business.

Step by step
To is for action. CC is for information. BCC keeps addresses private.
Start with a specific subject line. Hello tells the reader nothing. Request for invoice, Main Hall booking, 29 March, tells them everything before they open it.
Then the body has five parts. First, the greeting. Dear Mrs Okoro for formal, or Good morning Tunde for a known contact.
Second, one sentence saying why you are writing.
Third, only the details the reader needs, in short paragraphs or a list.
Fourth, a clear request: what you want and by when, ideally as a question.
Fifth, your signature: full name, role, business name and phone number. Mention and clearly name every attachment.
Put the person who must act in the To line, and people who only need to know in CC.

Honest promises and private data
Check stock, time and cash before you promise
Say what you can do, and when
Do not share customers' numbers or chats
Give bad news early, with a new plan
A written promise is something the customer plans around. Check your stock, time and cash before you commit.
Instead of, no problem, 500 packs by Friday, say: we can deliver 300 by Friday and the other 200 by Tuesday.
Nigeria's Data Protection Act 2023 sets rules for personal data. Collect only what you need, keep it secure, and never post screenshots showing customers' names or numbers.
And if a delivery will be late, say so early, with the reason and your new plan. Silence and excuses do far more damage.

Higher-stakes communication

Every business negotiates all the time: with suppliers on price, with landlords on rent, with customers on discounts.
Good negotiation is not shouting or tricks. It is mostly preparation, listening and clear communication.
You will also learn to adjust when your reader comes from a different culture or time zone.
And you will bring everything together in a capstone with measured results.
Before you negotiate
Target: the realistic result you aim for
Walk-away point: beyond this you say no
Opening offer: close enough to be serious
BATNA: what you will do if there is no deal
Before an important negotiation, write down your target: the realistic result you are aiming for.
Your walk-away point: the worst deal you will accept. Beyond this, you say no.
Your opening offer: where you start, close enough to be taken seriously.
And your BATNA, which means best alternative to a negotiated agreement. It is what you will do if there is no deal.
The stronger your alternative, the more confidently you can negotiate.
Worked example
Zainab negotiates a fabric price
Prepare: target 8,200, walk away at 8,600
Open: 50 pieces a month at 8,000?
Listen: what would help you most?
Trade: full payment on collection
Agree at 8,300 and confirm in writing
Trade concessions. Never give a discount for nothing.
For example, Zainab makes dresses in Kaduna and pays about 9,000 naira per piece of Ankara. These prices are illustrative.
Her target is 8,200 and her walk-away is 8,600. Her alternative is another wholesaler who quoted 8,500, with slower delivery.
She opens: I plan to order 50 pieces every month instead of 20. Could you do 8,000 per piece?
The wholesaler says that is too low. Zainab asks, what would help you most? He says payment on time and fewer small orders.
That is his interest. His position was the price. His interest is reliable payment.
So she offers to pay in full on collection and order once a month.
They settle at 8,300 naira. That saves her 35,000 naira a month on 50 pieces.
She sends a WhatsApp summary of the deal the same day.
Notice that Zainab traded something for every step down in price. A common mistake is giving a discount and asking nothing in return.
Across cultures
In high-context settings, much of the meaning is in the relationship and what is not said. Many West African business settings lean this way.
In low-context settings, people expect meaning in the words themselves. Neither is better. These are tendencies, not rules about every person.
So if a partner says, we will try our best, ask gently: should I plan for Friday or the following week? And with second-language readers, use short sentences and no slang like no wahala.
Time zones
Chiamaka books a call with New York
Nigeria is on WAT, with no clock changes
New York in winter: 6 hours behind
Pick an overlap: 3pm WAT is 9am New York
State both times, check a world clock app
For calls abroad, always state both times.
For example, Chiamaka exports shea butter from Abuja and needs a call with a buyer in New York. Nigeria uses West Africa Time, W A T.
In winter, New York is six hours behind Nigeria.
Chiamaka works 9am to 6pm. She picks 3pm in Nigeria, which is 9am in New York, early in the buyer's day.
Her message states both times, and she checks them in a world clock app first.
Your capstone
Measure how your messages perform
Date, who, channel, purpose, reply or not, days to reply, and follow-up questions.
Replies divided by important messages sent. It should rise as your writing improves.
Replies that asked for something your message should have said. It should fall.
For your capstone, keep a communication log: a simple table where you record important messages and what happened.

Your response rate is the replies divided by the messages sent. For example, Ruth runs a cleaning service in Lagos. Before the course, 11 of her 20 messages got replies, 55%. After, 16 of 20, that is 80%.
Your clarification rate counts replies asking for missing details. Ruth's fell from about 55% to about 19%. That is honest evidence she can show a client or programme officer.
